| rf_ask_plain | Those same visitor instructions, then the data page, both requested under one fixed name. |
| rf_fail | It would record one of three things, named in the result: the host answered a refusal to this client's request for the robots.txt file; the robots.txt permits the client on the path and the host answered a refusal for that same path; or no robots.txt is served, which under the standard declares permission and involves no contradiction (the page may well have been served). Only the second is a host doing other than it declared; a rate-limit refusal may be temporary rather than a policy; a temporary error or server failure is never a fail here; and it is about one identified client, not every crawler. |
| rf_hypothesis | Does the host enforce what it declares? A host whose robots.txt permits an identified, compliant client and whose edge then refuses that client tells SI systems one thing and does another; the refusal, not the declaration, decides what they can read. |
| rf_name_brief | The site serves what its own rules permit |
| rf_not_measured | The public client could not settle the page, for one of three reasons: the host refused the identified client; the client's own robots.txt compliance kept it from reading; or it could not confirm an absence, or a server or network error stopped it — here, no response to either request or a server error on the page request. |
| rf_partial | This check is under review and is not scored yet, so no result is given. |
| rf_pass | This check is under review and is not scored yet. What it would record as a pass: the robots.txt permits this client on the data page's path and the host actually served the page to it. |
| rf_plain_name | Host serves the path its robots.txt permits |
| rf_question | Does the host actually serve the data page to an identified, compliant client when its own robots.txt says it may? |
| rf_requirements | [{"source": "rfc-9309-robots-exclusion-protocol", "quote": "These rules are not a form of access authorization."}, {"source": "rfc-9309-robots-exclusion-protocol", "quote": "The Robots Exclusion Protocol is not a substitute for valid content security measures."}, {"source": "rfc-9309-robots-exclusion-protocol", "quote": "then the crawler MAY access any resources on the server."}, {"source": "rfc-9309-robots-exclusion-protocol", "quote": "\"Unavailable\" means the crawler tries to fetch the robots.txt file and the server responds with status codes indicating that the resource in question is unavailable."}, {"source": "rfc-9309-robots-exclusion-protocol", "quote": "For example, in the context of HTTP, such status codes are in the 400-499 range."}] |

| rf_what_client_does | The public client asks for the robots.txt file, then asks for the data page itself as the same identified client, and compares what robots.txt permits with what the host actually served. |
| rf_where_we_look | At the site's robots.txt file and at the data page's web address, both requested as the same identified client. |
| rf_who_else | No public tool runs this exact check. |
| rf_why_it_matters | An RFC on robots.txt states that its rules are not a form of access authorization and are not a substitute for valid content security measures; the idea that a host's enforcement should match its declaration is this project's own construct. This check is under review and not scored yet. |

| rule_id | RULE-A12-v3 |
| signal | Per host: GET /robots.txt and parse it; then GET the product path under the identified UA. Coherent iff robots.txt permits the path for this UA AND the host serves it. Incoherent iff robots.txt permits and the host answers a status in `manners.unobservable_statuses` (401/403/407/429). A robots.txt that DISALLOWS the path is not incoherence — it is A4's measurement, and this indicator is `not_applicable` there. |

| candidate_rationale | The public-observable leg of A11's enforced layer. A11 places enforced and observed access at `agency_instrumented` because a WAF is not visible from outside; that holds in general and fails for the one case where robots.txt PERMITS a path and the host REFUSES a compliant client asking for it. The disagreement between the two declared and enforced layers is then observable at the public tier with no edge logs at all. |
